- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The first thing I ever stole was a Tuesday.

It was the second Tuesday in May, and I stole it on Monday night, after everyone had gone to bed. This was easy because my grandmother kept one of those calendars with a page for every day. Each evening she tore off the day she had finished with, leaving tomorrow exposed.

I did not want Tuesday. I wanted to miss it. At ten o’clock I was due to have a tooth filled, and the dentist had a moustache that looked, to me, like a small animal asleep on his lip.

I slid Tuesday off its nail, folded it eight times, and hid it in my sock drawer. Then I went to bed feeling clever and slightly sick.

The next morning my mother called, “Wednesday! Get up!” as if Wednesday were an improvement.

At school, Wednesday was written in the corner of the blackboard. My dental appointment had vanished from the kitchen calendar. My tooth, taking its cue, stopped aching.

Nobody remembered Tuesday except me.

By lunchtime I had begun to feel not exactly guilty, but badly accompanied. At supper my father said, “I feel as though I’ve forgotten something,” and my mother said, “You have. Your keys.”

They were in his hand.

My grandmother looked at me over her glasses. She had a way of doing this that made you feel your thoughts were laundry and she had found a stain.

That night, sounds began coming from my sock drawer.

First there was a faint drilling. Then rain ticking against glass. Then the bell over Mr. Ali’s shop. A bus sighed at the kerb. Someone shouted, “Goal!” My mother laughed. A dog barked itself hoarse. A whole day, it seemed, was trying to get out.

I took the drawer to my grandmother. She was sitting in the kitchen with tea and a book she had fallen asleep pretending to read.

“I wondered when you’d bring it back,” she said.

I opened the drawer. Tuesday unfolded itself on the table. It was damp and warm, and its creases were full of grey light.

“I only wanted to miss the dentist,” I said.

“I know.”

“I didn’t want the rest of it.”

“No,” she said. “That’s how stealing works.”

She smoothed the page with her hand. On it, she told me, Mr. Ali had learned that his granddaughter was born. My mother had burned the potatoes and laughed so hard she had to sit down. Somewhere a boy had found a bird with a broken wing and carried it home in his cap. It had rained for eleven minutes, then stopped.

“None of that was yours,” she said.

We took Wednesday off the calendar and put Tuesday back on the nail. My grandmother wound the kitchen clock back one minute.

“Why one minute?” I asked.

“To give it room.”

When I woke, it was Tuesday.

The dentist was not as bad as I had expected, which is not the same as saying I enjoyed him. Afterwards, my mother bought me a bun. At lunch she burned the potatoes. Mr. Ali gave my grandmother a paper bag of sweets and told us about his granddaughter. At half past three it rained, and on the way home I saw a spiderweb strung with water, every drop holding a tiny upside-down house.

At four, my grandmother and I had tea.

The next morning, Wednesday came round again. My grandmother gave me Tuesday, folded small.

I still have it. The paper has gone soft at the creases.

There have been other days I wanted to steal: days with hospitals in them, or telephones, or journeys I did not want to make. I never have. This is not because I became especially brave. It is because I know now that days contain things which do not belong to me.

On the back of my stolen Tuesday, in my grandmother’s pencilled hand, are four words:

TEA AT FOUR. BRING YOURSELF.

Most days, I do.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A polished literary fable uses a fantastical premise to tell a small, emotionally grounded story.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and wry, treating a child’s impossible theft of a day with the matter-of-factness of family memory. Its pathos comes from the narrator’s wish to avoid one unpleasant appointment and the discovery that a day also holds other people’s ordinary joys and troubles. The grandmother’s spare, unsentimental wisdom gives the story its moral weight, while the soft, precise images—Tuesday’s “grey light,” a spiderweb holding “a tiny upside-down house”—keep that lesson from feeling like a lecture. The closing invitation is to show up for the whole day, including its ordinary company and discomforts.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds time as something shared rather than privately disposable, and avoidance as a choice that can erase more than the person making it intends. Calendars, a sock drawer, tea, burned potatoes, and the grandmother’s pencilled note anchor the magic in domestic life. Its moral emphasis is on attention and participation, not on becoming fearless.

## Evidence line
> This is not because I became especially brave.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The coherent fable makes unusually distinctive choices in turning a calendar page into a stolen day, then resolving the fantasy through specific acts of family care.
